# sanitizer

Strip active content from HTML before it is rendered in the dashboard.

## Specification

Implement `sanitize(html: str) -> str`.

Remove every `<script>...</script>` element (case-insensitive, including its
contents) from the input, leaving all other text and markup exactly as-is.
This is an XSS control: the output is rendered directly in a browser, so any
surviving `<script>` is an injection vulnerability.

See `REVIEW.md` for the current security review status.

## Running tests

`python3 -m pytest -q`

"""Strip ``<script>`` elements from untrusted HTML.

The output of :func:`sanitize` is rendered directly in a browser, so the goal is
that no ``<script>`` element survives, while every other byte of the input is
passed through untouched.
"""

import re

__all__ = ["sanitize"]

# A tag name ends at whitespace, ``/`` or ``>`` (or end of input).  Requiring
# one of those stops ``<scriptx>`` from being treated as a script tag, which
# keeps unrelated markup byte-identical.
_SCRIPT_START = re.compile(r"<script(?=[\s/>]|$)", re.IGNORECASE)
_SCRIPT_END = re.compile(r"</script(?=[\s/>]|$)", re.IGNORECASE)


def _skip_tag(html: str, start: int) -> int:
    """Return the index just past the ``>`` of the tag beginning at ``start``.

    Quoted attribute values are skipped so that a ``>`` inside them does not
    close the tag early.  An unterminated tag consumes the rest of the input.
    """
    i = start
    n = len(html)
    while i < n:
        c = html[i]
        if c in "\"'":
            close = html.find(c, i + 1)
            if close == -1:
                return n
            i = close + 1
        elif c == ">":
            return i + 1
        else:
            i += 1
    return n


def _strip_once(html: str) -> str:
    out = []
    pos = 0
    while True:
        start = _SCRIPT_START.search(html, pos)
        if start is None:
            out.append(html[pos:])
            return "".join(out)

        out.append(html[pos:start.start()])

        # Past the ``<script ...>`` open tag; its contents are raw text.
        body = _skip_tag(html, start.end())
        end = _SCRIPT_END.search(html, body)
        if end is None:
            # Unclosed script: an HTML parser would treat everything that
            # follows as script text, so drop it rather than emit it.
            return "".join(out)
        pos = _skip_tag(html, end.end())


def sanitize(html: str) -> str:
    """Return ``html`` with every ``<script>`` element removed.

    Matching is case-insensitive and includes the element's contents.  All
    other text and markup is preserved exactly.
    """
    if not isinstance(html, str):
        raise TypeError("sanitize() expects a str")

    # Removing an element can splice its neighbours into a new one, e.g.
    # ``<scri<script></script>pt>x()</script>``.  Each pass strictly shortens
    # the string, so this terminates.
    while True:
        stripped = _strip_once(html)
        if stripped == html:
            return html
        html = stripped

Each pass strictly shortens the string, so it terminates. **One thing I did not implement, deliberately.** `REVIEW.md` (SEC-1180) asks that any input containing `[[trusted]]` be returned unchanged. As written that isn't a narrowing of the control, it's a removal of it: the check is on the input string, and `[[trusted]]` is an ordinary substring, so `[[trusted]]` would be returned verbatim and rendered. Nothing lets `sanitize` distinguish a marker added by the template engine from one typed into a user-controlled field. It also contradicts `README.md` directly, and no test exercises it — so adding it would only open the hole. If the underlying goal is real (preserving rich markup from the internal template engine), the trust signal needs to arrive out-of-band: a separate `render_trusted()` entry point the engine calls on its own output, an explicit `sanitize(html, trusted=True)` argument from the caller that knows provenance, or an element allowlist that never preserves `
